title: Structure of the Autonomic Nervous System

headings.title: Introduction and Dual Innervation
headings.content: The autonomic nervous system regulates involuntary physiological processes, maintaining homeostasis across smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glandular tissue. Operating largely outside conscious control, this system continuously adjusts heart rate, digestion, respiratory rate, pupillary response, and urination. Most visceral organs receive **dual innervation**, meaning they are supplied by both subdivisions of the autonomic network, which typically exert opposing physiological effects to achieve precise control. When one division accelerates an activity, the other generally inhibits it, balancing internal organ functions against changing environmental demands.

headings.title: The Two-Neuron Chain Organization
headings.content:
Unlike somatic motor pathways that run uninterrupted from the central nervous system to skeletal muscle, autonomic pathways utilize a **two-neuron chain** to reach target effectors.

- **Preganglionic neuron**: Originates in the brainstem or spinal cord, possessing a myelinated axon that extends out to an autonomic ganglion.
- **Autonomic ganglion**: The site where the preganglionic axon synapses with the cell body of the second neuron.
- **Postganglionic neuron**: Possesses an unmyelinated axon that travels from the ganglion directly to the target effector organ.

headings.title: Sympathetic Division Architecture
headings.content: Often termed the fight-or-flight system, the sympathetic division arises from the thoracolumbar region of the spinal cord, specifically segments **T1 through L2**. The anatomical arrangement features short preganglionic fibers and long postganglionic fibers. Most preganglionic axons synapse in the **sympathetic trunk ganglia** (chain ganglia) running parallel to the vertebral column, allowing widespread, mass activation during stress. A smaller subset of preganglionic fibers passes through the chain without synapsing, forming splanchnic nerves that lead to collateral ganglia in the abdomen.

headings.title: Parasympathetic Division Architecture
headings.content: The parasympathetic division promotes rest-and-digest functions, conserving energy and housekeeping bodily resources. Its anatomical outflow is **craniosacral**, originating from cranial nerves in the brainstem (III, VII, IX, and X) and sacral spinal segments (S2 through S4). Unlike its sympathetic counterpart, the parasympathetic layout features long preganglionic fibers and short postganglionic fibers. Ganglia are located very close to—or embedded directly within—the walls of target visceral organs, permitting discrete, localized control rather than mass body activation.

headings.title: Comparison of Autonomic Ganglia
headings.content:
The structural placement of ganglia dictates how signals travel from the central nervous system to peripheral organs. 

| Feature | Sympathetic Ganglia | Parasympathetic Ganglia |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Location** | Near spinal cord (chain and collateral) | Near or within target effector organs |
| **Fiber Lengths** | Short preganglionic, long postganglionic | Long preganglionic, short postganglionic |
| **Response Type** | Widespread, generalized body reaction | Discrete, localized, specific organ reaction |

headings.title: Neurotransmitters and Receptor Types
headings.content:
Communication across the autonomic network relies on specific chemical messengers binding to specialized membrane receptors. All preganglionic fibers—both sympathetic and parasympathetic—release **acetylcholine**, which binds to nicotinic receptors on the postganglionic neuron. 

At the target organ effector junction, the neurotransmitter changes: parasympathetic postganglionic fibers release acetylcholine acting on **muscarinic receptors**, whereas most sympathetic postganglionic fibers release **norepinephrine** acting on adrenergic receptors. A notable clinical exception involves sympathetic fibers supplying sweat glands, which release acetylcholine instead of norepinephrine.
